drills.coachNote: White's knight on e5 wants to jump to g6, forking your queen on e7 and rook on f8 — right now your f7 pawn is the only thing stopping that, since it guards g6. Playing f6 pushed that guard out of the way, so Ng6 landed with a fork, your queen had to flee with Qf7, and Nxf8 Rxf8 cost you a rook for a knight, nearly four pawns of your edge gone. Rfe8 avoids all that: it contests the e-file, and after Nf3 Qd7 Qd2 Rxe1+ Rxe1 you simplify cleanly. Don't move a pawn that's guarding a key square until you've checked what it opens.

drills.coachNote: White is happy to meet a knight on d4 with Nxd4, trading pieces open, and then swing his queen to g4 — dangerous because your king is still sitting on e8, not yet castled. That's exactly what Nd4 invited: Nxd4 exd4 Qg4, and suddenly the queen is eyeing your weakened kingside, so you had to scramble with Qf6 just to hold on, giving back most of a two-pawn edge. Ne7 instead develops quietly, covers d5 and f5, and after c4 g6 Qb3 Rb8 d4 you're still solid and ready to tuck your king away. When your king's still home, don't trade into lines that open toward it.

drills.coachNote: White's e-pawn is one step from e5, and pushing it with a knight sitting on f6 comes with free tempo, forcing you to react on his terms. Bb4+ flips the script: it's check, so if White blocks with Nc3 you just take it, Bxc3+, and after bxc3 Qxc3+ Kf2 you've won the knight while keeping your queen barking checks at his exposed king. drills.coachNote: There's no real counterplay here — White's king is stuck in the corner with g3, h3, and Rh1 blocking every square it could run to, and your rook on f2 already controls f1 and g2's neighbor squares. You still won the game, but it's worth training the eye to scan for mate before grabbing material whenever the enemy king looks this boxed in.

drills.coachNote: Black's plan is the same skewer idea as before: get the queen to c2, check along the second rank, and win the rook on d1 if nothing stands between it and your king. Right now f2 is the pawn plugging that rank. Playing f3 pulls it off entirely, so Qc2+ works at once — Kh3, Qxd1, and the rook's gone again. Rd4 sidesteps all of it by getting the rook off the rank and active instead, and after Rd4 Ke6 Rf4 a5 Kg3 you're repositioning safely while Black just pushes pawns. Keep an eye on which of your own pawns are quietly blocking checks before you move them.
drills.threat: Your pawn on f2 is the only thing blocking Black's queen from checking on c2 along the second rank.

drills.explanation: Re2 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Kf3 ran into Bd5+, costing about 17.3 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs koleapapa (479) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Black's queen on d2 has you in check along the second rank, and the real danger is his bishop on f7 sitting on the same diagonal that runs through d5 toward your king. Kf3 gets you out of check but walks right onto that diagonal — Bd5+ forces Be4 to block, then Bxe4+ just wins your bishop with another check, torching the edge you had. Re2 solves it properly: it blocks the check and invites Qxe2+ Bxe2 trading queens, then Nxf7 Kxf7 mops up Black's bishop too, leaving you clearly up material. When you're in check, look at blocking before you run the king onto a diagonal an enemy bishop already covers.
drills.threat: You're in check from Black's queen on d2 along the second rank, and his bishop on f7 watches the diagonal to your king too.

drills.explanation: Qf7 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Qxc5 ran into f4+, costing about 12.9 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs koleapapa (479) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Black's king on h8 is nearly boxed in, with your knight on e5 covering key flight squares, so there's a bigger prize available than the pawn on c5. Qxc5 grabs it but gives Black a breather: f4+ kicks your king, gxf4 forces you to spend a move recapturing, and b6 then chases your queen off c5, handing him activity he shouldn't get. Qf7 instead keeps the king pinned down and the pressure constant — after Qf7 Rb8 Nd7, your knight jumps even deeper into his position while the attack keeps building. When you're already crushing and the enemy king is stuck, finish the attack before cashing in loose pawns.
drills.threat: Black's king on h8 has barely any squares left, and your knight on e5 already covers key escapes around it.

drills.explanation: Bd7 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Nh6 left that piece hanging: after Qxh6 it's simply lost.
drills.title: vs magdyis (520) — Grob Opening
drills.coachNote: White's queen on c1 sits on the c1-h6 diagonal, waiting for something undefended to land on it — and since your g-pawn already moved to g6, h6 is wide open. Nh6 drops the knight right into that line with zero protection, so Qxh6 just wins it outright, and after Bd7 Qg7 Rf8 the queen digs in for even more, turning an even game clearly worse. Bd7 was the move instead: it develops a piece without touching that diagonal, and after Bd7 Rg3 c5 Qf4 Qc7 Qg5 you're simply developing while White's idea goes nowhere. Before placing a piece, check which open lines it lands on, especially ones aimed at the enemy queen.
drills.threat: White's queen on c1 points straight down the long diagonal to h6, and anything undefended that lands there is free.

drills.explanation: Qh4+ forks the king on e1 and the king on e1 — one of them falls next move. In the game, Rd2 ran into Nxe3, costing about 5.0 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs magdyis (520) — Grob Opening
drills.coachNote: White's king is still stuck on e1, your pawn on e3 is one step from tearing open f2, and your queen on h6 can join in with checks — that's your real weapon here. Rd2 looks natural, lining the rook against the queen on g2, but it lets White play Nxe3: after Rxg2 Nxg2, he's traded his queen for your rook and pawn, a swap that actually favors him and lets the attack fizzle. Qh4+ keeps it going instead — Nf2 is forced, exf2+ wins the knight with check, and Kf1 Rd1+ Ke2 crashes your rook straight into his king. When attacking an exposed king, keep forcing checks rather than quietly repositioning.
drills.threat: White's king is still stuck on e1 with nowhere safe to go, and your pawn on e3 is one step from ripping open f2.
